                         REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF
                DEEP SOUTH CENTER FOR ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE

        Pursuant to Section 19(a) of the Natural Gas Act Section 19(a)1 and Rule 713 of the Rules

of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission2 (“Commission” or

“FERC”), Deep South Center for Environmental Justice (“DSCEJ”) hereby requests rehearing of

the Order Issuing Certificates and Approving Abandonments issued by the Commission on

September 10, 2026, authorizing construction and operation of the Kosciusko Junction Pipeline

Project (“Project”).3 The Commission granted DSCEJ’s motion to intervene in this proceeding.4

Thus, DSCEJ is a party to the proceeding and has standing to file this request for rehearing.5 The

request is timely, having been filed on the first day that is not a weekend day or legal holiday

thirty days after the Certificate Order.6

                                             BACKGROUND


        On September 12, 2025, Gulf South Pipeline Company, LLC (“Gulf South”) and Texas

Gas Transmission, LLC (“Texas Gas”) (collectively, “Applicants”) submitted a joint application

(“Application”) for a certificate of public convenience and necessity seeking approval for the

Kosciusko Junction Pipeline Project (“Project”), which would allow Applicants to construct and

operate 110 miles of new pipeline and related facilities, acquire and abandon approximately 98

miles of existing pipeline, and install new or modified aboveground facilities in Washington,

Sunflower, Humphreys, Holmes, Attala, Leake, Newton, Jasper, and Clarke counties, in

Mississippi.7 The Applicants proposed an in-service date of “no later than April 1, 2029.”8

        Section 7(e) of the Natural Gas Act (“NGA”) obligates the Commission to ensure that

any proposed gas infrastructure is justified by market need and is required by the “present or

future public convenience or necessity.”9 The Commission must consider all relevant evidence of

alleged market need beyond precedent agreements, particularly where independent evidence

       As outlined and discussed further below, FERC’s Certificate Order finding project need

contains several reversible errors. Errors include: failure to establish a genuine need for the

Project and arbitrary reliance on the existence of precedent agreements that are not dispositive of

need; improper disregard of substantial evidence concerning speculative demand, existing

capacity, and costs that may be shifted to captive ratepayers; failure to meaningfully weigh the

Project’s claimed benefits against its harms; approving the Project based on an incomplete

environmental review that failed to adequately analyze harms to landowners, communities, air

quality, and public health; and improperly disregarding important comments and expert analyses,

including disregard of substantial evidence of harm to local communities most impacted by the

Project.

       The Commission’s errors violated the Natural Gas Act (“NGA”), National Environmental

Policy Act (“NEPA”), and the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”). The Commission’s

assessment of the Project’s impacts fell well short of its obligations under NEPA, subsequently

compromising its balancing of public benefits and adverse effects pursuant to the NGA. The

Certificate Order evidences arbitrary and capricious and unreasoned decision-making in

contravention of the APA. Before irreparable harm befalls the communities alongside the

                         CONCISE STATEMENT OF ALLEGED ERRORS12


     I. The Commission arbitrarily and capriciously authorized an unneeded gas pipeline project

     in violation of the Natural Gas Act (“NGA”) and Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”).

     FERC failed to fulfill its duty to only approve projects that are required by the public

     convenience and necessity, and protect consumers against corporate exploitation and the

     overbuilding of gas infrastructure. Substantial record evidence undermining the probative

     value of the Applicant’s assertions of need was before FERC, yet FERC arbitrarily

     disregarded and failed to meaningfully consider this evidence, and refused to look beyond the

     Applicant’s precedent agreements in the authorization of the Project. The Commission’s

     Certificate Order violates the NGA and the APA and is not the product of reasoned decision-

     making because of these failures and because the record does not contain substantial

     evidence supporting FERC’s finding that the Project is required by the public convenience

     and necessity.13

                                               ARGUMENT

I.      FERC’s Authorization of the Unneeded Project is Arbitrary, Capricious, a Violation
        of the NGA, the APA, and Otherwise Contrary to Law

     A. FERC failed to meaningfully and independently assess the Project’s stated need,
        and instead adopted the Applicants’ assertions

        The Applicants presented a market study, contested by commentors, purporting to

demonstrate need for the Project.21 The Commission concluded that FERC’s “determination of
